L111: ## Arrays
L112: 
L113: For a list of all array functions, see the 【80†array functions】 chapter in the documentation.
L114: 
L115: An 【81†array】 in PHP is actually an ordered map. A map is a type that associates values to keys. This type is optimized for several different uses; it can be treated as an array, list (vector), hash table (an implementation of a map), dictionary, collection, stack, queue, and probably more. As 【81†array】 values can be other 【81†array】s, trees and multidimensional 【81†array】s are also possible.
L116: Explanation of those data structures is beyond the scope of this manual, but at least one example is provided for each of them. For more information, look towards the considerable literature that exists about this broad topic.
L117: ### Syntax
L118: #### Specifying with 【82†array()】
L119: 
L120: An 【81†array】 can be created using the 【82†array()】 language construct. It takes any number of comma-separated `key => value` pairs as arguments.
L121: 
L122:     array(
L123:         key  => value,
L124:         key2 => value2,
L125:         key3 => value3,
L126:         ...
L127:     )
L128: The comma after the last array element is optional and can be omitted. This is usually done for single-line arrays, i.e. `array(1, 2)` is preferred over `array(1, 2, )`. For multi-line arrays on the other hand the trailing comma is commonly used, as it allows easier addition of new elements at the end.
L129: 
L130: > Note:
L131: >
L132: > A short array syntax exists which replaces `array()` with `[]`.
L133: Example #1 A simple array
L134: 
L135:     `<?php
L136:     $array1 = array(
L137:         "foo" => "bar",
L138:         "bar" => "foo",
L139:     );
L140: 
L141:     // Using the short array syntax
L142:     $array2 = [
L143:         "foo" => "bar",
L144:         "bar" => "foo",
L145:     ];
L146: 
L147:     var_dump($array1, $array2);
L148:     ?>`
L149: 
L150: The key can either be an 【83†int】 or a 【84†string】. The value can be of any type.
L151: 
L152: Additionally the following key casts will occur:
L153:   * 【84†String】s containing valid decimal 【83†int】s, unless the number is preceded by a `+` sign, will be cast to the 【83†int】 type. E.g. the key `"8"` will actually be stored under `8`. On the other hand `"08"` will not be cast, as it isn't a valid decimal integer.
L154: 
L155:   * 【85†Float】s are also cast to 【83†int】s, which means that the fractional part will be truncated. E.g. the key `8.7` will actually be stored under `8`.
L156:   * 【86†Bool】s are cast to 【83†int】s, too, i.e. the key `【87†true】` will actually be stored under `1` and the key `【88†false】` under `0`.
L157: 
L158:   * 【89†Null】 will be cast to the empty string, i.e. the key `【90†null】` will actually be stored under `""`.
L159: 
L160:   * 【81†Array】s and 【77†object】s can not be used as keys. Doing so will result in a warning: `Illegal offset type`.
L161: 
L162: If multiple elements in the array declaration use the same key, only the last one will be used as all others are overwritten.
L163: Example #2 Type Casting and Overwriting example
L164: 
L165:     `<?php
L166:     $array = array(
L167:         1    => "a",
L168:         "1"  => "b",
L169:         1.5  => "c",
L170:         true => "d",
L171:     );
L172:     var_dump($array);
L173:     ?>`
L174: 
L175: The above example will output:
L176: 
L177:     array(1) {
L178:       [1]=>
L179:       string(1) "d"
L180:     }
L181: 
L182: 
L183: As all the keys in the above example are cast to `1`, the value will be overwritten on every new element and the last assigned value `"d"` is the only one left over.
L184: PHP arrays can contain 【83†int】 and 【84†string】 keys at the same time as PHP does not distinguish between indexed and associative arrays.
L185: 
L186: Example #3 Mixed 【83†int】 and 【84†string】 keys
L187: 
L188:     `<?php
L189:     $array = array(
L190:         "foo" => "bar",
L191:         "bar" => "foo",
L192:         100   => -100,
L193:         -100  => 100,
L194:     );
L195:     var_dump($array);
L196:     ?>`
L197: The above example will output:
L198: 
L199:     array(4) {
L200:       ["foo"]=>
L201:       string(3) "bar"
L202:       ["bar"]=>
L203:       string(3) "foo"
L204:       [100]=>
L205:       int(-100)
L206:       [-100]=>
L207:       int(100)
L208:     }
L209: 
L210: 
L211: The key is optional. If it is not specified, PHP will use the increment of the largest previously used 【83†int】 key.
L212: 
L213: Example #4 Indexed arrays without key
L214: 
L215:     `<?php
L216:     $array = array("foo", "bar", "hello", "world");
L217:     var_dump($array);
L218:     ?>`
L219: The above example will output:
L220: 
L221:     array(4) {
L222:       [0]=>
L223:       string(3) "foo"
L224:       [1]=>
L225:       string(3) "bar"
L226:       [2]=>
L227:       string(5) "hello"
L228:       [3]=>
L229:       string(5) "world"
L230:     }
L231: 
L232: 
L233: It is possible to specify the key only for some elements and leave it out for others:
L234: 
L235: Example #5 Keys not on all elements
L236: 
L237:     `<?php
L238:     $array = array(
L239:              "a",
L240:              "b",
L241:         6 => "c",
L242:              "d",
L243:     );
L244:     var_dump($array);
L245:     ?>`
L246: The above example will output:
L247: 
L248:     array(4) {
L249:       [0]=>
L250:       string(1) "a"
L251:       [1]=>
L252:       string(1) "b"
L253:       [6]=>
L254:       string(1) "c"
L255:       [7]=>
L256:       string(1) "d"
L257:     }
L258: 
L259: 
L260: As you can see the last value `"d"` was assigned the key `7`. This is because the largest integer key before that was `6`.
L261: 
L262: Example #6 Complex Type Casting and Overwriting example
L263: This example includes all variations of type casting of keys and overwriting of elements.
L264: 
L265:     `<?php
L266:     $array = array(
L267:         1    => 'a',
L268:         '1'  => 'b', // the value "a" will be overwritten by "b"
L269:         1.5  => 'c', // the value "b" will be overwritten by "c"
L270:         -1 => 'd',
L271:         '01'  => 'e', // as this is not an integer string it will NOT override the key for 1
L272:         '1.5' => 'f', // as this is not an integer string it will NOT override the key for 1
L273:         true => 'g', // the value "c" will be overwritten by "g"
L274:         false => 'h',
L275:         '' => 'i',
L276:         null => 'j', // the value "i" will be overwritten by "j"
L277:         'k', // value "k" is assigned the key 2. This is because the largest integer key before that was 1
L278:         2 => 'l', // the value "k" will be overwritten by "l"
L279:     );
L280: 
L281:     var_dump($array);
L282:     ?>`
L283: The above example will output:
L284: 
L285:     array(7) {
L286:       [1]=>
L287:       string(1) "g"
L288:       [-1]=>
L289:       string(1) "d"
L290:       ["01"]=>
L291:       string(1) "e"
L292:       ["1.5"]=>
L293:       string(1) "f"
L294:       [0]=>
L295:       string(1) "h"
L296:       [""]=>
L297:       string(1) "j"
L298:       [2]=>
L299:       string(1) "l"
L300:     }
L301: 
L302: 
L303: Example #7 Negative index example
L304: When assigning a negative integer key `n`, PHP will take care to assign the next key to `n+1`.
L305: 
L306:     `<?php
L307:     $array = [];
L308: 
L309:     $array[-5] = 1;
L310:     $array[] = 2;
L311: 
L312:     var_dump($array);
L313:     ?>`
L314: 
L315: The above example will output:
L316: 
L317:     array(2) {
L318:       [-5]=>
L319:       int(1)
L320:       [-4]=>
L321:       int(2)
L322:     }
L323: 
L324: 
L325: Warning
L326: Prior to PHP 8.3.0, assigning a negative integer key `n` would assign the next key to `0`, the previous example would therefore output:
L327: 
L328:     array(2) {
L329:       [-5]=>
L330:       int(1)
L331:       [0]=>
L332:       int(2)
L333:     }
L334: #### Accessing array elements with square bracket syntax
L335: 
L336: Array elements can be accessed using the `array[key]` syntax.
L337: 
L338: Example #8 Accessing array elements
L339: 
L340:     `<?php
L341:     $array = array(
L342:         "foo" => "bar",
L343:         42    => 24,
L344:         "multi" => array(
L345:              "dimensional" => array(
L346:                  "array" => "foo"
L347:              )
L348:         )
L349:     );
L350: 
L351:     var_dump($array["foo"]);
L352:     var_dump($array[42]);
L353:     var_dump($array["multi"]["dimensional"]["array"]);
L354:     ?>`
L355: The above example will output:
L356: 
L357:     string(3) "bar"
L358:     int(24)
L359:     string(3) "foo"
L360: 
L361: 
L362: > Note:
L363: >
L364: > Prior to PHP 8.0.0, square brackets and curly braces could be used interchangeably for accessing array elements (e.g. `$array[42]` and `$array{42}` would both do the same thing in the example above). The curly brace syntax was deprecated as of PHP 7.4.0 and no longer supported as of PHP 8.0.0.
L365: Example #9 Array dereferencing
L366: 
L367:     `<?php
L368:     function getArray() {
L369:         return array(1, 2, 3);
L370:     }
L371: 
L372:     $secondElement = getArray()[1];
L373: 
L374:     var_dump($secondElement);
L375:     ?>`
L376: 
L377: > Note:
L378: >
L379: > Attempting to access an array key which has not been defined is the same as accessing any other undefined variable: an `【91†E_WARNING】`-level error message (`【92†E_NOTICE】`-level prior to PHP 8.0.0) will be issued, and the result will be `【90†null】`.
L380: > Note:
L381: >
L382: > Array dereferencing a scalar value which is not a 【84†string】 yields `【90†null】`. Prior to PHP 7.4.0, that did not issue an error message. As of PHP 7.4.0, this issues `【92†E_NOTICE】`; as of PHP 8.0.0, this issues `【91†E_WARNING】`.
L383: #### Creating/modifying with square bracket syntax
L384: 
L385: An existing 【81†array】 can be modified by explicitly setting values in it.
L386: 
L387: This is done by assigning values to the 【81†array】, specifying the key in brackets. The key can also be omitted, resulting in an empty pair of brackets (`[]`).
L388: 
L389:     $arr[key] = value;
L390:     $arr[] = value;
L391:     // key may be an 【83†int】 or 【84†string】
L392:     // value may be any value of any type
L393: If `$arr` doesn't exist yet or is set to `【90†null】` or `【88†false】`, it will be created, so this is also an alternative way to create an 【81†array】. This practice is however discouraged because if `$arr` already contains some value (e.g. 【84†string】 from request variable) then this value will stay in place and `[]` may actually stand for 【93†string access operator】. It is always better to initialize a variable by a direct assignment.
L394: > Note:
L395: >
L396: > As of PHP 7.1.0, applying the empty index operator on a string throws a fatal error. Formerly, the string was silently converted to an array.
L397: 
L398: > Note:
L399: >
L400: > As of PHP 8.1.0, creating a new array from `【88†false】` value is deprecated. Creating a new array from `【90†null】` and undefined values is still allowed.
L401: 
L402: To change a certain value, assign a new value to that element using its key. To remove a key/value pair, call the 【94†unset()】 function on it.
L403: Example #10 Using Square Brackets with Arrays
L404: 
L405:     `<?php
L406:     $arr = array(5 => 1, 12 => 2);
L407: 
L408:     $arr[] = 56;    // This is the same as $arr[13] = 56;
L409:                     // at this point of the script
L410: 
L411:     $arr["x"] = 42; // This adds a new element to
L412:                     // the array with key "x"
L413: 
L414:     unset($arr[5]); // This removes the element from the array
L415: 
L416:     var_dump($arr);
L417: 
L418:     unset($arr);    // This deletes the whole array
L419: 
L420:     var_dump($arr);
L421:     ?>`
L422: > Note:
L423: >
L424: > If no key is specified, the key will be the maximum existing integer index + `1`. If the array has no positive integer indices, the key will be `0`. As of PHP 8.3.0, it can also be a negative integer.
L425: >
L426: > Note that the maximum integer key used for this need not currently exist in the 【81†array】. It need only have existed in the 【81†array】 at some time since the last time the 【81†array】 was re-indexed. The following example illustrates:
L427: >
L428: >     `<?php
L429: >     // Create a simple array.
L430: >     $array = array(1, 2, 3, 4, 5);
L431: >     print_r($array);
L432: >
L433: >     // Now delete every item, but leave the array itself intact:
L434: >     foreach ($array as $i => $value) {
L435: >         unset($array[$i]);
L436: >     }
L437: >     print_r($array);
L438: >
L439: >     // Append an item (note that the new key is 5, instead of 0).
L440: >     $array[] = 6;
L441: >     print_r($array);
L442: >
L443: >     // Re-index:
L444: >     $array = array_values($array);
L445: >     $array[] = 7;
L446: >     print_r($array);
L447: >     ?>`
L448: >
L449: > The above example will output:
L450: >
L451: >     Array
L452: >     (
L453: >         [0] => 1
L454: >         [1] => 2
L455: >         [2] => 3
L456: >         [3] => 4
L457: >         [4] => 5
L458: >     )
L459: >     Array
L460: >     (
L461: >     )
L462: >     Array
L463: >     (
L464: >         [5] => 6
L465: >     )
L466: >     Array
L467: >     (
L468: >         [0] => 6
L469: >         [1] => 7
L470: >     )
L471: >
L472: #### Array destructuring
L473: 
L474: Arrays can be destructured using the `[]` (as of PHP 7.1.0) or 【95†list()】 language constructs. These constructs can be used to destructure an array into distinct variables.
L475: 
L476: Example #11 Array Destructuring
L477: 
L478:     `<?php
L479:     $source_array = ['foo', 'bar', 'baz'];
L480: 
L481:     [$foo, $bar, $baz] = $source_array;
L482: 
L483:     echo $foo, PHP_EOL;    // prints "foo"
L484:     echo $bar, PHP_EOL;    // prints "bar"
L485:     echo $baz, PHP_EOL;    // prints "baz"
L486:     ?>`
L487: Array destructuring can be used in 【96†`foreach`】 to destructure a multi-dimensional array while iterating over it.
L488: 
L489: Example #12 Array Destructuring in Foreach
L490: 
L491:     `<?php
L492:     $source_array = [
L493:         [1, 'John'],
L494:         [2, 'Jane'],
L495:     ];
L496: 
L497:     foreach ($source_array as [$id, $name]) {
L498:         echo "{$id}: '{$name}'\n";
L499:     }
L500:     ?>`
L501: 
L502: Array elements will be ignored if the variable is not provided. Array destructuring always starts at index `0`.
L503: Example #13 Ignoring Elements
L504: 
L505:     `<?php
L506:     $source_array = ['foo', 'bar', 'baz'];
L507: 
L508:     // Assign the element at index 2 to the variable $baz
L509:     [, , $baz] = $source_array;
L510: 
L511:     echo $baz;    // prints "baz"
L512:     ?>`
L513: 
L514: As of PHP 7.1.0, associative arrays can be destructured too. This also allows for easier selection of the right element in numerically indexed arrays as the index can be explicitly specified.
L515: Example #14 Destructuring Associative Arrays
L516: 
L517:     `<?php
L518:     $source_array = ['foo' => 1, 'bar' => 2, 'baz' => 3];
L519: 
L520:     // Assign the element at index 'baz' to the variable $three
L521:     ['baz' => $three] = $source_array;
L522: 
L523:     echo $three, PHP_EOL;  // prints 3
L524: 
L525:     $source_array = ['foo', 'bar', 'baz'];
L526: 
L527:     // Assign the element at index 2 to the variable $baz
L528:     [2 => $baz] = $source_array;
L529: 
L530:     echo $baz, PHP_EOL;    // prints "baz"
L531:     ?>`
L532: Array destructuring can be used for easy swapping of two variables.
L533: 
L534: Example #15 Swapping Two Variable
L535: 
L536:     `<?php
L537:     $a = 1;
L538:     $b = 2;
L539: 
L540:     [$b, $a] = [$a, $b];
L541: 
L542:     echo $a, PHP_EOL;    // prints 2
L543:     echo $b, PHP_EOL;    // prints 1
L544:     ?>`
L545: 
L546: > Note:
L547: >
L548: > The spread operator (`...`) is not supported in assignments.
L549: > Note:
L550: >
L551: > Attempting to access an array key which has not been defined is the same as accessing any other undefined variable: an `【91†E_WARNING】`-level error message (`【92†E_NOTICE】`-level prior to PHP 8.0.0) will be issued, and the result will be `【90†null】`.
L552: 
L553: > Note:
L554: >
L555: > Destructuring a scalar value assigns `【90†null】` to all variables.
L556: ### Useful functions
L557: 
L558: There are quite a few useful functions for working with arrays. See the 【80†array functions】 section.
L559: > Note:
L560: >
L561: > The 【94†unset()】 function allows removing keys from an 【81†array】. Be aware that the array will not be reindexed. If a true "remove and shift" behavior is desired, the 【81†array】 can be reindexed using the 【97†array_values()】 function.
L562: >
L563: > Example #16 Unsetting Intermediate Elements
L564: >
L565: >     `<?php
L566: >     $a = array(1 => 'one', 2 => 'two', 3 => 'three');
L567: >
L568: >     /* will produce an array that would have been defined as
L569: >        $a = array(1 => 'one', 3 => 'three');
L570: >        and NOT
L571: >        $a = array(1 => 'one', 2 =>'three');
L572: >     */
L573: >     unset($a[2]);
L574: >     var_dump($a);
L575: >

L580: The 【96†`foreach`】 control structure exists specifically for 【81†array】s. It provides an easy way to traverse an 【81†array】.
L581: ### Array do's and don'ts
L582: #### Why is `$foo[bar]` wrong?
L583: 
L584: Always use quotes around a string literal array index. For example, `$foo['bar']` is correct, while `$foo[bar]` is not. But why? It is common to encounter this kind of syntax in old scripts:
L585: 
L586:     `<?php
L587:     $foo[bar] = 'enemy';
L588:     echo $foo[bar];
L589:     // etc
L590:     ?>`
L591: This is wrong, but it works. The reason is that this code has an undefined constant (`bar`) rather than a 【84†string】 (`'bar'` - notice the quotes). It works because PHP automatically converts a bare string (an unquoted 【84†string】 which does not correspond to any known symbol) into a 【84†string】 which contains the bare 【84†string】. For instance, if there is no defined constant named `bar`, then PHP will substitute in the 【84†string】 `'bar'` and use that.
L592: 
L593: Warning
L594: The fallback to treat an undefined constant as bare string issues an error of level `【92†E_NOTICE】`. This has been deprecated as of PHP 7.2.0, and issues an error of level `【91†E_WARNING】`. As of PHP 8.0.0, it has been removed and throws an 【98†Error】 exception.
L595: 
L596: This does not mean to always quote the key. Do not quote keys which are 【8†constants】 or 【7†variables】, as this will prevent PHP from interpreting them.
L597: Example #17 Key Quoting
L598: 
L599:     `<?php
L600:     error_reporting(E_ALL);
L601:     ini_set('display_errors', true);
L602:     ini_set('html_errors', false);
L603: 
L604:     // Simple array:
L605:     $array = array(1, 2);
L606:     $count = count($array);
L607: 
L608:     for ($i = 0; $i < $count; $i++) {
L609:         echo "\nChecking $i: \n";
L610:         echo "Bad: " . $array['$i'] . "\n";
L611:         echo "Good: " . $array[$i] . "\n";
L612:         echo "Bad: {$array['$i']}\n";
L613:         echo "Good: {$array[$i]}\n";
L614:     }
L615:     ?>`
